listen: Good morning. This is The Daily Brief for Wednesday, October 28. Our lead story today is the Israeli election. The BBC reports that the two main blocs appear to have too few seats to form the next government without relying on Arab parties. Netanyahu and Eisenkot are both set to fall short of victory. That means Arab parties could hold the key to any coalition. Now the front page. The Lever has read the paperwork for Anthropic's proposed public offering. It says the filing reveals key weaknesses, including a blackmail warning. Separately, Anthropic says it is committing a portion of its shares to a new entity called the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Its stake increases as the company grows. In football, the 49ers have traded for defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, continuing a run of reunions with former players. And in health news, the Ebola outbreak that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now counted ten thousand patients. It has spread with great speed. Now the sections. In tech, Anthropic is expanding its partnership with the General Services Administration to bring Claude to all levels of government. A trending framework called Superpowers offers a development method for coding agents. And Simon Willison has been hacking on a conference badge at GitHub Universe. In politics, Drop Site News reports that groups aligned with AIPAC are spending seven hundred eighty five thousand dollars on late attack ads in a California House race. A new NPR poll shows Democrats with an edge a week before Election Day. And a federal judge has barred more work at a Washington golf course site, while President Trump says he will appeal. In world news, a ceasefire has been extended across Ukraine's Kherson region. The United States will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family. And a cruise ship has ended its long voyage over fuel costs. In sports, one analysis grades the Buckner trade and other deals ahead of the NFL deadline. A UFC Fight Night in Sydney will feature Quillan Salkilld against Benoît Saint Denis. And ESPN looks back at the first week of the NBA season. In Atlanta, ground has broken on another Beltline segment. A historic Westside movie theater is moving ahead with a mixed-use revival. And Georgia's early voting has passed two million. In architecture, AEC Magazine asks how far Autodesk wants to own the new computing stack. There is also a mass timber pavilion in Los Angeles, and reflections from the Buenos Aires biennial. In science, Curiosity is preparing to drill at a site called Nazca. Brain implants are turning attempted speech into words. And four volunteers will leave a yearlong Mars simulation on Saturday. That is the brief. Have a good day.

lead.title: Arab parties could hold key as Netanyahu and Eisenkot set to fall short of victory
lead.note: Israel's election has not produced a clear winner. The BBC reports that the two main blocs appear to have too few seats to form the next government without relying on Arab parties. Netanyahu and Eisenkot are both set to fall short of victory, according to the report. That places Arab parties in a position that could prove decisive in any attempt to put a coalition together. No seat counts are given, so the exact balance between the blocs is not yet clear. For a reader following world news, the key point is that the vote has left the question of who governs open, and the talks that follow will matter as much as the ballots themselves. It is worth watching how the bloc negotiations develop in the coming days.
lead.headline: Israel's Vote Leaves No Clear Winner
decks: Netanyahu and Eisenkot both appear set to fall short of victory.
Neither main bloc has enough seats without Arab parties.
Arab parties could hold the key to forming a government.
